messages.subject: Poisson vs binary models under non-Poisson counts
messages.subject_clean: Poisson vs binary models under non-Poisson counts
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

In the Royle et al (2014) SCR textbook, I noticed that the authors recommend turning count detection data into binary responses and fitting a binary-response model (Section 9.1.3, pp 249--250). The rationale is that if you get the response distribution for the counts wrong, then your model is misspecified in some way, and this may affect point estimates and CIs; using binary data may result in a more robust model. While this throws away some information, in many cases it seems that the differences in precision between count and binary models are fairly small if the counts are truly Poisson (e.g., Appendix A in Efford et al, 2009, Population density estimated from locations of individuals on a passive detector array).

I have a student learning to use the secr package, so as an exercise I had them investigate the affects of non-Poisson counts on estimator properties. I had a hunch that assuming a Poisson distribution when the counts were in fact overdispersed might result in CI coverage less than the nominal level (as is the case for a standard GLM), and vice-versa for underdispersion. Surprisingly, CI coverage appeared more or less spot on the nominal levels for Poisson models when the data were moderately overdispersed.

The upshot of all this is that it doesn't appear to matter much whether you fit binary or Poisson response models, even when the counts are moderately overdispersed; it seems you get more or less the right result, and both point and variance estimator properties between the two are similar. Has anyone else observed this result? Appendix A in the Efford et al (2009) paper above describes models with a negative binomial response, but it doesn't seem to simulate non-Poisson data to test their performance vs standard Poisson-count models.

Finally, we briefly thought about trying to fit a negative binomial response, but there appears to be a bug in secr.fit():

library(secr)
detectors  <- make.grid (nx = 10, ny = 10, spacing = 20,
                         detector = "count")
detections <- sim.capthist (detectors, noccasions = 1,
    popn = list(D = 5, buffer = 100),
    detectpar = list(g0 = 0.9, sigma = 25))
mask <- make.mask (detectors, buffer = 100, nx = 48)
## Works fine with binomN >= largest detection count.
secr.model <- secr.fit (detections, mask = mask, binomN = max(detections), trace = FALSE)
## Error with negative binomial response.
secr.model <- secr.fit (detections, mask = mask, binomN = -1, trace = FALSE)

The first model works as one would expect, but the second throws the following error:

Error in (function (f, p, ..., hessian = FALSE, typsize = rep(1, length(p)),  :
  missing value in parameter
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In autoini(ch, msk, binomN = details$binomN, ignoreusage = details$ignoreusage) :
  'autoini' failed to find g0; setting initial g0 = 0.1
2: In log(x) : NaNs produced

Given the second warning, my guess is that there is a missing check for a negative binomN, and that there should be something like:

if (binomN < 0){
  [Do negative binomial stuff]
} else {
  [Do binomial stuff]
}

I can see how a bug might creep in, as I don't expect many people use the negative binomial option in secr.fit().

Thanks for any insight!

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben

I hadn't read that advice in Royle et al. (2014) but it fits my intuition and it's good to have some confirmation that modelling binary proximity data doesn't sacrifice much. Of course, just how much is lost depends on the sparseness of the data (often most of the animal x site x occasion counts are just 0 or 1). As 'secr' is coded at present, Poisson count models are also _much_ slower to fit than binary models. One context in which count data can really matter is with sightings of unmarked animals - reducing these to binary at the level of site x occasion can sacrifice a lot of information, but in that situation I particularly distrust the independence assumption, so binary may still be best. (And I've seen others resort to binary when MCMC struggled with counts).

As you suggest, the negative binomial option in 'secr' is seldom used, and in fact is completely stuffed in the current version. It crept into the code long ago when I was just playing with possibilities. Note that the size parameter always had to be specified - it was not estimated. When I try it (bypassing autoini by specifying start values) I get errors like negative binomN not allowed in C fn pndot, which is explicit. So the reference to the negative binomial in the help for secr.fit is a significant documentation bug that I'll fix ASAP. Sorry for leading you astray. The alternative of fixing this limited implementation of the negative binomial does not appeal because (i) there hasn't yet been a case made that it helps in practice (ii) the negative binomial is so often a dog to fit (iii) the code within 'secr' has got lot more complex to handle occasion-specific detectors, mark-resight etc. I could be persuaded if there was a need.

Cheers
Murray

Hi Murray,

Great, thanks for the quick and informative response. Regarding "I could be persuaded if there was a need", my student's simulations suggest that fitting a Poisson model appears to work perfectly fine, even when the response data are truly negative binomial---so this seems like a fairly good reason not to bother!

I'm still a little perplexed as to why CIs are still sound under a violated Poisson assumption. Perhaps I am missing something obvious, or perhaps this is another case of the seemingly remarkable robustness of SECR to some assumption violations.

Cheers,

Ben

messages.body_plain:
The concern raised in the SCR book is the potential lack of independence in the counts that would obscure the relationship between the distance from the activity center to the trap and the recorded counts.  For example, if we assume a continuous time movement model centered around the activity center, more counts will be recorded when the animal is in the vicinity of the trap than when it is not.  Then without conditioning on the location of the animal when the counts were recorded, they are no longer iid with respect to the overall activity center.  This could lead to overdispersion in the counts, but I think your simulations with overdispersion don't fully mimic the situation of lack of independence.  It would be interesting to see some simulations with lack of independence in the count model.

messages.body_plain:
Another way to look at it is the number of counts conditional upon visiting a trap vs. the probability of visiting a trap.  It's reasonable to assume that the number of counts conditional upon visiting a trap is independent of the probability of visiting a trap (as specified by the distance-based detection function).  If all animals only visit the trap once during an occasion (seems frequent in practice), the counts above 1 tell you nothing about where the activity center is.  If they visit multiple times, then the counts above 1 are a noisy indicator of where the activity center is with more noise as lambda grows.  Here, the overdispersion model makes sense, but I'm not sure if it fully captures the effect of non-independence.

Back to the continuous time movement, if an animal traverses it's home range slowly relative to the length of a capture occasion, counts across occasions at the same trap will be more dependent than if an animal traverses it's home range quickly relative to the length of a capture occasion.  But the same applies to the binomial model, so maybe the overdispersion simulations are a good comparison when assuming independent trap visits.

Hi Ben,

Thanks for all that. I guess I should have clarified that we weren't considering discrete occasions---we only had one count for each individual/detector pairing, so you can consider our counts as being a sum for each individual/detector pairing across all 'occasions'.

It's not totally clear what you mean by 'lack of independence' in your first email, as SCR has various independence assumptions. You could be referring to the violation of one of two assumptions made by 'standard' SCR models:
Conditional on the activity centre, counts of detections across occasions are assumed to be independent and perhaps with the same encounter rate. This assumption ignores that the expected count varies depending on whether the animal is 'in the vicinity' on that given occasion.
Conditional on the activity centre, an animal's counts across detectors within an occasion are assumed to be independent. This assumption ignores that the expected counts across nearby traps are related; if you are 'in the vicinity' of one trap, then you are also 'in the vicinity' of another nearby trap.
If (1), I think we are roughly mimicking the 'lack of independence', partly by taking an overall count instead of artificially discretising things into occasions. The negative binomial distribution can be seen as a gamma-Poisson mixture, where you (1) generate a value mu from a gamma distribution, and (2) generate the resulting count from a Poisson distribution with expectation mu. So, detectors with high values of this latent gamma variate could be considered traps that the animal has been 'in the vicinity of' (in terminology of your first email) or 'visited' (in the terminology of your second email), while those with a low latent gamma variate are those that the animal has not.

If (2), of course our simple simulation was not quite as complex as throwing a movement model in the mix, which is a related can of worms. I am actually talking about something related to this at the upcoming EURING conference (apologies for the shameless self-promotion).

By the way, could you provide a reference for the continuous-time movement model in SCR you mentioned? I've seen movement models across discrete occasions (the transience and dispersal stuff). I have thought about how a continuous-time model might be fitted, but I've never tried because it sounds difficult---so this is relevant to my interests!

Thanks,

Ben

P.S. Perhaps this is getting off-topic. Happy to take this discussion off the list.

If all animals only visit the trap once during an occasion (seems frequent in practice), the counts above 1 tell you nothing about where the activity center is.  If they visit multiple times, then the counts above 1 are a noisy indicator of where the activity center is with more noise as lambda grows.  Here, the overdispersion model makes sense, but I'm not sure if it fully captures the effect of non-independence.

> > > > In addition: Warning messages:

> > > >   'autoini' failed to find g0; setting initial g0 = 0.1
> > > > 2: In log(x) : NaNs produced
> > > >
> > > > Given the second warning, my guess is that there is a missing check for a negative binomN, and that there should be something like:
> > > >
> > > > if (binomN < 0){
> > > >   [Do negative binomial stuff]
> > > > } else {
> > > >   [Do binomial stuff]
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > I can see how a bug might creep in, as I don't expect many people use the negative binomial option in secr.fit().

Kyle

The idea is to associate a set of trap covariates with occasions, and to give the set a name that can be used in a model formula. The specification is saved by 'timevaryingcov' as an attribute of the traps object. In your case I hope this will work:
timevaryingcov(traps(dataset)) <- list(bait = 1:6)
fit  <-secr.fit(dataset, model=list(D~1, g0~bait, sigma~1), buffer = 20000, trace = FALSE)
(associates the first 6 trap covariates with the name 'bait').

It is possible you will run into trouble with multiple sessions, but I hope it works as shown. Unfortunately, using any trap covariates down the fitting (I've lacked motivation to work on speeding it up).
Murray

Yes, I think my two emails were each only addressing one of those two independence assumptions so I wasn't being consistent or clear.  The second email was addressing concern 1 and I concluded that this violation would not be unique to the Poisson observation model so is not a reason to prefer the binomial model.  So I think the only relevant concern is the second one regarding independence within an occasion.  It seems like this would be a problem if the number of counts conditional upon visiting a trap is not related to distance to activity center and there are usually only single visits to each trap on each occasion.  Or thinking about it another way, if there are repeat visits to the same trap while the animal is in the vicinity of the trap and this is unrelated to the distance to the activity center.

To my knowledge, no SCR paper has used a continuous time movement model, although there are a couple that model detections in continuous time.  Richard Chandler has worked on an SCR model with an explicit movement model, but I don't think it's been published yet.

http://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0176966
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12196/full

>
> It's not totally clear what you mean by 'lack of independence' in your first email, as SCR has various independence assumptions. You could be referring to the violation of one of two assumptions made by 'standard' SCR models:
> Conditional on the activity centre, counts of detections across occasions are assumed to be independent and perhaps with the same encounter rate. This assumption ignores that the expected count varies depending on whether the animal is 'in the vicinity' on that given occasion.
> Conditional on the activity centre, an animal's counts across detectors within an occasion are assumed to be independent. This assumption ignores that the expected counts across nearby traps are related; if you are 'in the vicinity' of one trap, then you are also 'in the vicinity' of another nearby trap.
> If (1), I think we are roughly mimicking the 'lack of independence', partly by taking an overall count instead of artificially discretising things into occasions. The negative binomial distribution can be seen as a gamma-Poisson mixture, where you (1) generate a value mu from a gamma distribution, and (2) generate the resulting count from a Poisson distribution with expectation mu. So, detectors with high values of this latent gamma variate could be considered traps that the animal has been 'in the vicinity of' (in terminology of your first email) or 'visited' (in the terminology of your second email), while those with a low latent gamma variate are those that the animal has not.
>
> If (2), of course our simple simulation was not quite as complex as throwing a movement model in the mix, which is a related can of worms. I am actually talking about something related to this at the upcoming EURING conference (apologies for the shameless self-promotion).
>
> By the way, could you provide a reference for the continuous-time movement model in SCR you mentioned? I've seen movement models across discrete occasions (the transience and dispersal stuff). I have thought about how a continuous-time model might be fitted, but I've never tried because it sounds difficult---so this is relevant to my interests!

It's reasonable to assume that the number of counts conditional upon visiting a trap is independent of the probability of visiting a trap (as specified by the distance-based detection function).  If all animals only visit the trap once during an occasion (seems frequent in practice), the counts above 1 tell you nothing about where the activity center is.  If they visit multiple times, then the counts above 1 are a noisy indicator of where the activity center is with more noise as lambda grows.  Here, the overdispersion model makes sense, but I'm not sure if it fully captures the effect of non-independence.

messages.subject: Accounting for compromised baited traps and also incorporating natural "traps"
messages.subject_clean: Accounting for compromised baited traps and also incorporating natural "traps"
messages.body_plain:
In a bear molecular-mark recapture study, we are using baited barbed-wire corrals. The two bait types are occasion-specific covariates.

Rarely, bears/cows would knock down part of the barbed wires. We still get data from the traps, so we don't want to treat the trap as inactive. However, we would like to downweight their usage. Perhaps giving normal traps an "effort" of 1 and compromised traps an "effort" of 0.5? It happened very rarely and we doubt it would make much a difference in estimates, but it could. The traps were checked every 7 days and we don't know which day the trap was compromised. Thoughts?

Additionally, we have located a few trees where bears naturally rub. We are considering throwing out the "captures" from tree rubs because they we only have data from 4 tree rubs, compared to ~100 traps, but they could potentially be a good source of recaptures in our current study and in future studies as we find more and more. I was going to try treating these rubs as a separate trap, but I'm worried about ascertainment bias. They also differ from the baited "proximity" traps because they don't have any bait. Therefor, I'm not sure how to classify their "usage" and trap covariates. Each trap was checked over 6 occasions, including the rubs. Any advice on how to incorporate them into secr, or whether I should just throw them out, would be appreciated.

Others can comment if they've seen conflicting results, but in simulations I've done with *random* trap failure and scheduled trap replacement (e.g. camera traps that fail and are fixed when checked), fitting models ignoring the inactive traps did not introduce bias or reduce coverage.  The typical way this is modeled is using a trap operation file, but in the case where traps were turned of at random, it just reduced the estimate of p0 and reduced the precision of D a bit.  I suspect if traps are made less effective at random, the same result would hold.

messages.subject: Re: subsetting capture history
messages.subject_clean: subsetting capture history
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ujjwal
I think it would help to know more about your problem and why you want to do this. In general, I don't remember coding exactly what you ask for (spatial subset operation for polygon data), and it might be a little tricky. You could achieve the same result by first discretizing the polygon capthist (see ?discretize) and then subsetting using the traps argument (see ?subset.capthist), applying a criterion for whether each notional discretized trap was inside your desired area (see rough example code below). Masks are a different concept and probably not useful.
discreteCH <- discretize(polyCH, spacing = 500)  # choose spacing for your animal
newCH <- subset(discreteCH, traps = pointsInPolygon(traps(discreteCH), newpoly))
Regards
Murray

messages.subject_clean: Photo tagging approach for SMR of group living species using remote cameras
messages.body_plain:
I’m trying to estimate densities using a SMR framework for group living species (elk) using remote cameras. A portion of the population has uniquely marked collars. I have a question regarding photo tagging.

 I am getting lots of photos of multiple individuals on a single photograph, and many photos of the same group of individuals over a short period of time. Imagine a group of elk milling around the camera location for roughly half hour at a time with individuals entering and leaving the frame within the half hour period. I am wondering which photo tagging approach would be better:

1) Tag number of individuals on each individual photo
2) Tag number of individuals on each sequence of photos of the same group of animals during the same time period. This would require treating detections of a group of elk as a single “event”, and counting the numbers of individuals in each “event”

Does anyone have any insight on which approach would be better in a SMR framework? Thanks very much for the assistance.

messages.body_plain:
This seems like a difficult problem.  There is a severe lack of independence between the observations of the different animals because they move around in herds.  Further, the activity centers may be spatially clustered due to the herding behavior, but maybe not if they switch herds often.  I haven't seen anyone tackle these two problems but would be interested if someone has.

I suspect the lack of independence is even more of a problem in an SMR model because the underestimated uncertainty in the detection function parameters coming from the lack of independence will propagate less uncertainty into the estimated number of unmarked individuals that produced the unmarked counts you observed.  Thus the variance of the density estimator will be further underestimated.  And the lack of independence should lead to negative bias if it behaves like the lack of independence between multiple marking methods (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/eap.1587/full).

I think you need to model the observation process in a manner that accounts for the lack of independence, but I don't have any ideas about how to do that.

Hi,

The lack of independence due to clustered activity centres is equivalent to the problem in acoustic SCR whereby calls from the same animal have the same source location. This issue does not appear to affect point estimates of call density, but results in underestimated variance estimates (e.g., confidence intervals have less than their nominal coverage). This is mentioned in this paper <http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12291/full>, which also describes how you can obtain appropriate variance estimates via simulation, but this requires that you have external information about herd size (for clustered activity centres due to herds) or call rates (for clustered sound sources in acoustic SCR). This solution is not entirely satisfactory given the requirement for this external information. However, I have semi-developed methods for things that work if you can recognise which herd an animal comes from (for clustered activity centres due to herds), or if you can recognise which calls come from the same animal (for clustered sound sources in acoustic SCR).

Anyway, just thought I'd mention that there are probably solutions to this problem, but none are currently available, as far as I am aware!

Cheers,

Ben
